🗣 Exercise B — Put the stages in the correct order

Without looking at the pictures, recall the logical sequence from planning to sentencing. Discuss using the linking words below.

i → a → g → e → b → c → f → h → d → j
research & plan → break in → leave scene → evade arrest → caught → charged → trial → plead → verdict → sentence.
Key collocations: charge sb WITH robbery · sentence sb TO years · plead guilty (no preposition).
3 Reading

The Hatton Garden Job

Read the text and answer the questions.

📰 Read — then discuss the questions
Not 1every bank robber gets caught but 2plenty of them do, and the men who carried out the Hatton Garden Job were no exception. The raid has been called ‘the largest burglary in English history’, but since the contents of 3every safety deposit box is a secret and since 4few of the victims told the police what had been taken, it’s impossible to know how much was stolen. What we do know is that the men who carried out the crime were unusual. 5All of the ringleaders were older than 60. In fact, 6most of the gang members were past retirement age and 7two of them had already served time in prison. 8Both of them had also been found guilty of armed robbery.
Q1 — How much was stolen? Why is it hard to know?
Q2 — What made this gang unusual?
Q3 — Does anything about this story surprise you?
Q1: Possibly £14 million — impossible to know because victims didn’t reveal contents & boxes are secret.
Q2: All ringleaders over 60, most past retirement age; two had prior convictions for armed robbery.
Q3: Open — probe: Does age change how you feel about the crime? Were they brave or reckless?
4 Discovery

Discover the rules yourself

Look at sentences from the text — what do you notice?

🔎 Guided discovery — Quantifiers

Read each sentence. Think about the question, then click Reveal to check.

“Not every bank robber gets caught, but plenty of them do.”
👉 Can you say “every of them”? Why not? What do you use instead? What does plenty of suggest — large or small amount?
Every cannot be followed by of + pronoun. Use all of them instead. Every always takes a singular noun: every robber, not every of them.

Plenty of = a large amount, more than enough.
“Few of the victims told the police what had been taken.”
👉 Is this a large or small number? Does it feel positive or negative? How would the meaning change with “a few of the victims”?
Few (no “a”) = hardly any — fewer than expected. Negative / disappointing.
A few = some, a small but sufficient number. More positive.
Compare: “Few people came” (disappointing) vs “A few people came” (at least some).
“All of the ringleaders were older than 60. Most of the gang members were past retirement age.”
👉 If all = 100%, what percentage does most suggest? Can you think of quantifiers that go between them on a scale?
All = 100%. Most = majority, more than half but not all.
Scale: all → most → many / a lot of → some → a few → few → none.
Many is more common in negatives & questions; a lot of works in all contexts.
“Both of them had also been found guilty of armed robbery.”
👉 How many people does both refer to? Can you use all here? What’s the negative of both for exactly two people?
Both = exactly two. You can’t use all for two — use both.
Pairs: both ↔ neither (zero of two)    either = one or the other.
“Did either escape? No, neither did — both were caught.”
📂 Now sort the expressions

Drag each expression into the correct box. You can drag them back to the pool to try again.

all of both every each most of plenty of many / much a lot of a few of few of a little little a couple of none of neither either no / any
▮ Total amounts
▮ Large amounts
▮ Small amounts
▮ Zero / Unspecified
Total (100%): all, both, each, every — every + singular noun only; both = exactly two.
Large: most, plenty of, a lot of, many, much — many/much more common in negatives & questions.
Small: some, a few, few, a little, little, several, a couple of — few/little without “a” = negative feel.
Zero: no, none of, any, either, neither — no cannot be followed by of + pronoun.
5 Grammar Practice

Choose the right quantifier

Six sentences — one correct option each.

✎ Select the correct quantifier

Click the correct option. Think: countable or uncountable? Positive or negative feel? Exactly two, or more?

  • the gang members were past retirement age, but not all of them.
  • The police recovered of the stolen jewellery — most of it was never found.
  • ringleaders had criminal records — there were exactly two of them.
  • There were gang members who managed to escape abroad before the arrests.
  • The trial attracted media attention — people couldn’t get enough of the story.
  • the victims knew exactly what had been stolen from their boxes.
1. Most of  |  2. little (uncountable, negative feel)  |  3. Both (exactly two)  |  4. a couple of  |  5. plenty of  |  6. None of (“No of” is wrong; “neither” = only two things)
6 Speaking

Reconstruct the heist

Use quantifiers to retell the story — no numbers allowed.

🔐 Fact cards — click to reveal

Reveal all six facts, then retell the story replacing every number with a quantifier expression.

👥 The gang
6 men. Most had known each other for decades and had previous convictions.
👴 Their age
Average age over 60. The oldest was 76. Nicknamed “the Bad Grandpas.”
🔨 The method
Lowered 40m down a lift shaft. Drilled through a 50cm concrete wall over a 3-day holiday weekend.
💵 The haul
Broke into ~70 of the 999 deposit boxes. At least £14 million in cash, gems and jewellery.
🔒 The arrests
All 6 arrested within weeks via CCTV. 4 pleaded guilty. 2 convicted after trial.
💳 Recovery
Only a small fraction recovered. Most jewellery has never been found.
6 men → several / a handful of  |  over 60 → most were well past retirement age  |  70 of 999 → some / a few dozen of the boxes  |  £14m → a huge amount of money  |  4 pleaded guilty → most pleaded guilty  |  fraction recovered → little of the stolen property was found.
🗣 Discussion
Was the sentence fair? Should age be taken into account in sentencing?
The story became a film (King of Thieves, 2018). Why do heist stories fascinate us?
